phase1.output: (Window with beautifully styled controls using inline CSS)
phase1.explanation:
Everything so far has been functional but plain — default gray buttons, default fonts. [[term:CSS styling]] is the paint job and signage for the storefront.

The quickest way in is node.setStyle("..."), an inline string of property-value pairs, e.g. "-fx-background-color: #4CAF50; -fx-text-fill: white;". [[key:notice the -fx- prefix on every property]] — that's not a typo, it's how JavaFX tells its own custom properties apart from real web CSS, which it deliberately does not fully implement. Most property names should still feel familiar if you've seen web CSS (font-size, padding, border-radius all have -fx- equivalents), but treat it as "CSS-inspired," not "CSS."

Inline setStyle() is fine for a one-off tweak, but for anything bigger, an external stylesheet — a .css file loaded with scene.getStylesheets().add("style.css") — separates appearance from logic the same way FXML (coming up in two lessons) separates layout from behavior. Selectors work by CSS class (.my-button { ... }, assigned in Java with node.getStyleClass().add("my-button")) rather than by element type, which keeps styling reusable across many nodes instead of repeated inline strings.

[[warn:cascade order still applies]] — if the same property is set both inline and in a stylesheet, [[key:the inline setStyle() call wins]], the same "more specific source overrides the general one" rule real CSS follows.

phase2.errorMessage: (Button appears with default color — CSS is ignored or not applied!)
phase2.explanation:
[[warn:the button shows up in JavaFX's plain default gray — the styling never applied]].

The most common cause is a typo or missing property in the -fx- style string that fails silently: [[key:JavaFX doesn't throw an exception for an unrecognized CSS property, it just ignores that one line and renders everything it did understand]]. A missing semicolon between two properties has the same effect — everything after the missing semicolon gets swallowed into one malformed declaration and dropped. Unlike a Java compile error, a broken style string gives you no stack trace to follow — just a control that stubbornly looks unstyled.

mcq.question:
A Button has both an external stylesheet rule (.my-btn { -fx-background-color: blue; }) applied via getStyleClass() AND an inline button.setStyle("-fx-background-color: red;") call. What color does the button actually render?

A) Blue — external stylesheets always take priority for maintainability
B) Red — inline setStyle() overrides the stylesheet rule, same cascade priority as web CSS
C) A compile error — a node can't have two conflicting style sources
D) JavaFX's default gray, since the conflict cancels both rules

phase4.selfChallenge:
Write a JavaFX program with:
1. A Label with style: font-size 18px, bold, blue text, padding 10px
2. A Button with style: green background, white text, rounded corners, padding 10px 20px
3. A TextField with style: light gray background, border, padding 8px
4. A VBox with style: background color #f5f5f5, padding 20px

Use inline CSS (setStyle()) for all styling.

phase5.trivia: [[fun:JavaFX CSS only supports a subset of real CSS]] — no flexbox, no CSS grid, no media queries. It borrows the syntax and the -fx- properties are deliberately CSS-flavored so anyone who's styled a webpage feels at home fast, but it's its own independent styling language underneath, tailored specifically to scene-graph nodes.
